newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Canadian writer Margaret Atwood wary of praise.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Canadian writer Margaret Atwood wary of praise.

text.p: Despite a career marked by international criticial acclaim including a nomination for Britain's prestigious Booker Prize for her latest novel, Canadian writer Margaret Atwood remains wary of praise.

Atwood shrugs off positive reviews for her new novel "Alias Grace," saying it means her next work will come under fire from critics in the jealous world of literature. "I got such good reviews on this book that I know the bushes will be filled with snipers for the next time round. It's inevitable," she said.

Short-listed for the Booker, "Alias Grace" is a fictional account of a 19th-century servant girl's trial and conviction for her role in the murder of her employer and his lover, a crime that scandalised Victorian Canada with its violence and sexuality. The novel explores a landscape of stiff morality and repressed desires where teenage servant girls eke out desperate lives in their employers' homes and younger sons of well-to-do British families live like bohemians in "the colonies."

It is a story Atwood, 57, has been familiar with for more than two decades, one she discovered while delving into the annals of a notable Canadian pioneer whose writings about life in early Canada were the inspiration for a book of poetry.

"I knew the story actually a very long time before I ever thought of writing a book about it," she told Reuters. "I had come across it because I was writing a series of poems called 'The Journals of Susanna Moodie'".

Although her book on Susanna Moodie's writings was published in the 1970s, Atwood said she was haunted by the story of the double murder and widening divisions between the historical reality of the murder case and the fanciful depictions that Moodie had given in her book, "Life in the Clearings."

The story, a departure from the feminist explorations in some of Atwood's other novels such as "Cat's Eye" and "The Robber Bride," tells Grace Marks' tale mostly from the celebrated murderess' own perspective. Atwood's treatment of Grace is a tantalizing page-turner that reveals more about the convicted murderess on each page but remains elusive on the burning question in every reader's mind: Did she do it?
Despite attempts by Simon Jordon, a young pioneer doctor dabbling in psychiatry, to unlock the mystery of Grace's guilt or innocence, Atwood keeps the prim but able Grace a step ahead.

Amid the hoopla surrounding her third Booker nomination, Atwood said she was not surprised to lose the prize in October to the eventual winner, Britain's Graham Swift. "I would have bet on Swift too because one of the judges said several months before the event, 'Put your money on Swift.'"

She likened the yearly prize, which carries a $32,000 cash award, to a druidic ritual where the Booker judges pick out six "innnocent and spotless lambs," which are invited to a feast where five are slaughtered and one takes away the prize.

"The very next day everybody spits on it (the winning lamb) and drives it out of the village and all the bad luck of the year goes with it and people feel cleansed and refreshed and ready to do it all over again next year."
LOVE OF READING LED TO CAREER

Atwood, known as "Peggy" to her friends, credits her fondness for words to a childhood divided between summers in the wilds of Quebec and winters in various Canadian cities. "I became a reading addict and remained so ever since."

She said in a 1995 speech that her literary career began at 16 when she crossed the schoolyard on her way home. "I was scuttling along in my usual furtive way, suspecting no ill, when a large invisible thumb descended from the sky and pressed down on the top of my head. A poem formed."

Her slight frame and impish demeanor belie a multitude of literary achievements and a formidable intellect that has crafted many books, plays, screenplays and radio and television scripts and has made her work required reading for Canadian students.

She has garnered Canadian and international awards, starting with her 1964 book of poetry, "The Circle Game," which won Canada's biggest literary prize, the Governor General's Award, when Atwood was a graduate student at Harvard.

She said she writes not for critical acclaim but because the stories choose her, often against her better judgment. "You do not write in order to win prizes. You write for the reader, whoever that reader may be. As I said to my English publisher, I've gotten more flowers for not winning the Booker than I would have got if I had won it."
